faqs.question: What should the contact page say first?
faqs.answer: The sequence. A parent is in the practice the same night, a teacher can run one activity, or a school hears back about whether a conversation is the right step. Say whether a person replies. Do not make a self-serve trial sound like a welcome call.

faqs.question: What should the form ask?
faqs.answer: Ask for role, grade or skill, and email, plus a rough class size for a teacher and whether a school needs a privacy review. Do not collect real student names on a public form. Ask anything else in the reply, after the note is real.

faqs.question: What should the button say?
faqs.answer: Start a class, start a trial, or request a school conversation, matching the door they chose. Submit is weaker. The thank-you state should continue that sequence, into the lesson or into a reply window you can keep.

markdown:
An education product contact page should tell a teacher or a parent with little time what happens after they reach out, how fast, and what to have ready. The action is to start a class or a trial. A form with ten fields is a way to lose them.

They already saw the learning moment, or they would not be here. The page should make the next step feel small and specific. A second pitch is an insult to the minute they have left.

## What happens next

Write the sequence above the form, in a few lines. A parent starts a trial and is in the practice the same night. A teacher starts a class and can run one activity before they decide. A school sends a note and hears back about whether a conversation is even the right step. Three doors can share a page if each door states its own sequence. One vague "we'll be in touch" covers none of them.

Say what the first session contains, again, briefly. The parent will finish one short practice. The teacher will see who is stuck. Do not promise a transformed classroom by Friday. Small and true is what gets the form sent. Large and fuzzy is what gets the tab closed.

Say whether a person is in the loop. A family trial might be self-serve, and you should say that so they do not wait for a welcome call that is not coming. A school conversation should name what the call is for: fit, privacy questions, and whether a pilot is real. It is not a custom demo of features you hope to build. Teachers who have sat through those demos are allergic to them. Tell the truth about the format.

One path per door. Do not put a form, a calendar, a chat, and an email with equal weight. Pick the path you watch. A backup address in the footer is fine if a person reads it. Four inboxes is how notes die.

## A response you can keep

If a human replies, publish a window you have actually kept. Two working days. The next school day. Whatever is true. "We respond instantly" is a slogan, and an auto-reply is not a response. Say what the automatic note does, and what the human note will add. A teacher who writes during a planning period needs to know whether to expect an answer before the unit starts.

Be plain when you are slow. Booking school conversations for a later month is a fact. A form that implies someone is waiting by the phone is a small lie. Small lies train this buyer to expect the product to overclaim too. If the trial is instant and the school path is slow, say both. Speed can differ by door. Pretending otherwise creates angry parents and confused principals.

Do not offer a faster reply for people who look important. The window is a standard. If you cannot meet it, lengthen the sentence on the page. Do not lengthen the form to compensate. A long form in a busy week means you asked them to work before you had time to read.

Same-day help inside the product is a different promise from the contact page. If a teacher in a live class can only reach a help doc, say that near the class start, not as a buried disappointment. The contact page is for before they begin, and for the school path. Do not make it sound like a hotline if it is not one.

## What to have ready

Ask for the minimum that changes the path. Role: parent, teacher, or school. The skill or grade. An email. For a teacher, a rough class size. For a school, whether a privacy review is required. That is enough to route them. Everything else can wait until they have seen the lesson.

Optional, and labeled optional: a note about what is not working in the current routine. A worksheet they hate. A unit that starts Monday. These help you reply like a person. They should not be required. A parent who only has the email and the child's grade should still be able to start a trial.

Say what you do not need. A purchase order. A full roster of real student names on a public form. A password. A forty-page brief. Student names on a marketing form are a privacy mistake, not a lead-quality tactic. Collect roster details inside the product, after an account exists, under the policy you linked.

Give them a sentence they can paste if the box is blank. "I teach fourth grade and I want to try one fractions activity with one class." "I want a ten-minute reading practice tonight and I do not want to teach it myself." Edges on the blank box lower the freeze. "Tell us about your learning journey" raises it.

## Why ten fields lose the class

Each field delays the learning moment. Name, email, role, and grade are plenty for a trial. Company, phone, job title, how you heard about us, school address, a file upload, a newsletter opt-in that is actually on, and a comment essay are how a signup becomes a CRM. The parent did not come to feed a CRM. They came to see if a child will do the practice.

[The W3C's WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is the floor for the fields you keep. Visible labels, not placeholders that vanish. Errors that say what to fix. A button that says Start a trial or Start a class, not Submit. Contrast and focus that work on a phone in daylight. An education form that fails those basics will lose teachers for reasons you will misread as lack of interest.

Do not make them create a password before they see a lesson, if you can let them into one activity first. Do not use a quiz that scores their school's "readiness." Do not put a captcha in front of a parent unless you have a real abuse problem. The friction budget belongs to the lesson, which is allowed to be demanding. The door is not.

If a school path needs more, ask it in the reply, after you know the note is real. Two questions in an email feel like care. Fifteen required fields feel like a filter built by someone who does not want a pilot.

## Class or trial, not a generic inbox

Use the verbs the rest of the site uses. Start a class. Start a trial. If this page is the school path, say Request a school conversation, and do not dress it as a trial. Mixed words at the last step make people wonder if they chose the wrong door. The button is the last piece of routing.

Under the button, restate the result. A parent is in the practice tonight, or they get a reply inside the window. A teacher can run the activity before a purchase order, if that is true. A school gets a reply that says whether you can help. People press buttons when the result is a scene. They hesitate when the result is a spinner and a newsletter.

The thank-you state has to continue the sequence. For a trial, put them in the lesson or give a single link that does. Do not dump them on the homepage. Do not start a five-email course in the same moment. For a school note, say the window again and what you will ask next. Silence after a send feels like a lost form.

Watch one inbox. Print one backup address if you need it, as text a person can copy. Do not split new families, teachers, press, and hello across badges if only one is staffed. A teacher will write to the wrong one, and you will call them a bad lead.

## One owner, then the product

Someone owns replies. A backup owns them when that person is teaching, out, or building. "Replied" means a sentence about their class or their child, not a calendar link with no context, and not a PDF of features. Record the role, the grade, and the skill so the next conversation does not make them repeat the form.

Once they start, this page is no longer the home of the relationship. The class lives in the product. Notes you owe a school can live in a calmer place than an inbox. On a Hanabi project, ongoing files and updates live in a client portal. Your customers need the equivalent inside the product: the roster, the lesson, the teacher view. The contact page should hand them to that, not try to be it.

Read the form against the last twenty real signups once a term. If you always ask a missing question, add it only if it changes the path. If you never use a field, delete it. The page should get shorter as you learn what a real teacher and a real parent need, not longer as the form tool offers more widgets.

Cut anything on this page that performs taste instead of explaining the next hour. A badge wall. A mission paragraph. A reel. The person is ready to begin. [What not to put on the site](/blog/what-not-to-put-on-the-site-for-an-education-product) is the next piece if those leftovers are still sitting under the form. A shorter page that tells the truth will beat a long one that tries to inspire them one more time.

If you want the path checked by a studio that builds the page and the product together, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the form you use today. The useful result is fewer fields, a window you can keep, and a start that lands in the lesson.
